title: Nandaka's full moon
hook: an elder teaches the nuns; they are satisfied like the full moon

segments.voice: Yesterday: khanti, patience, and Punna's ladder of what didn't happen. Your line: at least they didn't.

Mahapajapati Gotami comes to the Buddha again, this time with five hundred nuns, asking him to teach them. In the hundred and forty-sixth discourse, the senior monks have been taking turns teaching the nuns. It's the turn of an elder named Nandaka, and he doesn't want to go. The discourse doesn't say why. The Buddha asks Ananda whose turn it is, hears the answer, and turns to Nandaka himself: teach the nuns, Nandaka. Give them a talk on the teaching. So Nandaka goes.
screen: `FIVE HUNDRED NUNS ASK TO BE TAUGHT.` → `IT'S NANDAKA'S TURN.` → `HE DOESN'T WANT TO GO.`

segments.voice: He teaches by asking. Sisters, is the eye permanent or impermanent? Impermanent, venerable sir. And what's impermanent, is it pain or ease? Pain, venerable sir. Is it fit to be called mine, me, my self? No, venerable sir. Through all six senses, their objects, and their kinds of knowing. Then three pictures. An oil lamp is burning: the oil, the wick and the flame all change. Would anyone say its light stays the same forever? A great tree: its roots, trunk, branches and leaves all change. Would its shadow be permanent? And a skilled butcher with a sharp knife, separating the hide from the flesh without cutting either: that's wisdom, slicing cleanly through what binds the mind. The nuns are pleased. But the Buddha sees they're glad, not yet fulfilled. Teach them again tomorrow, Nandaka, the same way. So he does. Then the Buddha uses the moon. On the fourteenth night, nobody looking up doubts it: the moon isn't full yet. That was the nuns after the first talk. On the fifteenth, nobody doubts either: the moon is full. That's the nuns after the second. The text says the least of the five hundred had entered the stream. Look back at the week: many names for a bowl, a stranger in a potter's shed, the truths expounded, a robe made by hand, a dying giver, Punna going west. And now a reluctant teacher, sent back a second time, until the moon was full.
screen: `TEACHING BY QUESTIONS` · `A LAMP, A TREE, A SHARP KNIFE` · `GLAD, BUT NOT YET FULFILLED` · `THE FOURTEENTH, THEN THE FIFTEENTH` · then, large: `THE MOON IS FULL.`

segments.voice: Think of one small thing you know well, how to make rice, how to calm down before a call, one line from this path, and picture someone who'd benefit. Picture teaching it the way Nandaka did: asking, not lecturing, and willing to say it again if it hasn't landed. Then let the picture go, and rest with the breath.
Punna. Full: a reluctant elder named Nandaka teaches the nuns twice, and they go from nearly full, like the fourteenth night, to full, like the fifteenth. Today's word.
Your line: the moon is full. Sometimes a teaching needs a second night to land. A week done; see you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The monastic rules ask the nuns' community to receive instruction (ovada) from the monks every half-month, and MN 146 shows one such teaching, given by questions and answers.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. the nuns are pleased with Nandaka's talk, but you see they aren't yet fulfilled. what do you do?

tell the nuns to study on their own.
fork.reveal: Nandaka teaches again in the same way, and the nuns become like the moon on the fifteenth: full.

original.note: Pali punna: full. the moon of the fifteenth is full, and so are the nuns after the second talk.

trapdoor: what you thought: one good talk is enough.
what it means: the nuns were glad after the first and fulfilled after the second, like the moon going from nearly full to full.

what a scholar hears: MN 146, the Nandakovada Sutta, uses the uposatha moons of the fourteenth and fifteenth as its frame and states that the least of the five hundred bhikkhunis became a stream-enterer.
guess: full, like the moon on the fifteenth night
a monk who teaches the nuns their rules
a new moon, dark and hidden from view

chat.says: The nuns liked Nandaka's first talk. Why did the Buddha send him back again?
options: Glad isn't fulfilled: like the fourteenth moon, they needed one more night to be full.
His first talk was full of mistakes, so the Buddha made him go fix them.
The nuns complained about him, so the Buddha punished him with another turn.
chat.meaning: The Buddha saw the nuns were pleased but not yet fulfilled; after the second talk, like the moon on the fifteenth night, they were full.

Nandaka.meaning: an elder who taught the nuns, though reluctant

Punna.meaning: full; also the name of yesterday's monk

Mahapajapati Gotami.meaning: the Buddha's aunt and foster mother

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 146, Nandakovada Sutta (advice from Nandaka)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 'nobody says why' now 'the discourse doesn't say why' (the commentary does give a reason); howItsDone rewritten around the half-monthly instruction rule instead of unsourced 'often' and 'commonly' claims.
MN 146 paraphrased. Confirm: Mahapajapati with five hundred nuns, the rota of senior monks, Nandaka's reluctance, the lamp, tree and butcher similes, and the fourteenth/fifteenth moon simile.
Confirm the closing claim that the least of the five hundred became a stream-enterer.

Review pass: the fourteenth-night image was rewritten. The draft said people 'can't quite tell' whether the moon is full; as I recall MN 146, the point is that on the fourteenth nobody doubts it is not yet full, and on the fifteenth nobody doubts it is full. Confirm against the Pali.
